stem: Insectivorous plants such as the pitcher plant and Venus flytrap trap insects mainly to obtain
explanation: These plants are green and make their own sugar by photosynthesis, but they grow in nitrogen-poor soils, so they digest insects to obtain nitrogen. They do not depend on insects for energy.

stem: The digestion of starch begins in the mouth by the action of
explanation: Salivary glands secrete amylase (ptyalin), which starts breaking starch into maltose while food is chewed. Pepsin acts on proteins in the stomach, and trypsin and lipase work in the small intestine.

stem: In the stomach, the inactive enzyme pepsinogen is converted into active pepsin by
explanation: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen and parietal cells secrete HCl, which converts it into pepsin; pepsin itself then activates more pepsinogen. Enterokinase activates trypsinogen in the small intestine, not pepsinogen.

stem: Bile helps the digestion of fats because it
options: emulsifies fats into tiny droplets, increasing surface area for lipase
explanation: Bile, made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder, contains bile salts but no digestive enzymes; it breaks fat into small droplets so pancreatic lipase can act faster. Thinking bile contains lipase is the common mistake.

stem: In the villi of the small intestine, digested fats are mainly absorbed into the
explanation: Fatty acids and glycerol are reformed into fats inside the epithelial cells and enter the lacteal, a lymph vessel in the centre of each villus. Sugars and amino acids enter the blood capillaries and travel through the hepatic portal vein to the liver.

stem: Most peptic ulcers of the stomach and duodenum are now known to be linked with infection by the bacterium
explanation: Helicobacter pylori survives in the stomach lining and weakens its protective mucus, so acid and pepsin damage the wall. E. coli is a normal gut bacterium, and Vibrio cholerae causes cholera with watery diarrhoea, not ulcers.

stem: Stomata open in light because potassium ions are actively moved into the guard cells, which
options: raises their water potential, so water leaves and they become flaccid
makes the guard cells thinner on the inner wall
converts sugar into starch inside them
lowers their water potential, so water enters and they become turgid
explanation: Entry of K⁺ makes the guard cell sap more concentrated, so water moves in by osmosis; the thick inner walls bend as the cells swell and the pore opens. Water leaving makes the cells flaccid and closes the stoma, which is what happens in darkness.

stem: In human lungs, the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide takes place across the walls of the
explanation: Alveoli are tiny air sacs with very thin walls, a huge total surface and a dense network of capillaries, ideal for diffusion. The trachea and bronchi only conduct air, and the pleura surrounds the lungs.

stem: Most carbon dioxide is carried in the blood as hydrogencarbonate ions, which form mainly
options: in the plasma, without any enzyme
inside red blood cells, by the enzyme carbonic anhydrase
on the haem group of haemoglobin
inside white blood cells, by lipase
explanation: Carbonic anhydrase in red cells rapidly converts CO₂ and water into carbonic acid, which ionises into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻; the HCO₃⁻ then diffuses into the plasma in exchange for Cl⁻ (chloride shift). Only a small fraction of CO₂ binds haemoglobin, and it binds the protein part, not the haem.

stem: Carbon monoxide is poisonous because it
options: combines with haemoglobin far more firmly than oxygen does
explanation: CO binds haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, which is very stable, so less haemoglobin is free to carry O₂ and the tissues suffer oxygen lack. It does not burst red cells.

stem: In emphysema, breathing becomes difficult mainly because
options: the bronchi are blocked by a tumour
the pleural cavity fills with air
walls of the alveoli break down, reducing the surface for gas exchange
explanation: Long exposure to smoke damages the elastic alveolar walls, so many small alveoli merge into fewer large sacs with much less surface area. A blocking tumour describes lung cancer, and air in the pleural cavity is a collapsed lung.

stem: In flowering plants, water and dissolved minerals move up from the roots mainly through the
explanation: Xylem vessels and tracheids form continuous dead tubes that carry water and minerals upward. Phloem carries sugars and other organic food in translocation, which is the usual confusion.

stem: According to the cohesion-tension theory, water rises to the top of a tall tree mainly because
options: transpiration from leaves pulls a continuous column of water molecules held together by cohesion
root pressure pushes water to the top
phloem pumps water upward using ATP
water is absorbed directly by the leaves
explanation: Evaporation from leaf cells creates tension that pulls water up the xylem, and hydrogen bonding (cohesion) keeps the column unbroken. Root pressure exists but is far too weak to lift water up a tall tree.

stem: According to the pressure-flow (mass flow) hypothesis, phloem sap moves from a leaf to a root because
options: xylem pulls the sap down by transpiration
sugar loading at the leaf draws in water, building pressure that pushes sap towards the root where sugar is removed
gravity carries the sap down to the root
explanation: Sucrose loaded into sieve tubes at the source lowers water potential, so water enters from the xylem and hydrostatic pressure rises; at the sink sugar is unloaded, water leaves and pressure falls, so sap flows from high to low pressure. This is why phloem can carry sap upwards too, ruling out gravity.

stem: The natural pacemaker that starts each heartbeat is the
explanation: The SA node in the wall of the right atrium sends out impulses that spread over both atria, making them contract. The AV node, bundle of His and Purkinje fibres pass the impulse on to the ventricles but do not start it.

stem: Oxygenated blood from the lungs enters the heart through the
options: pulmonary arteries into the right atrium
venae cavae into the right atrium
pulmonary veins into the left atrium
explanation: Pulmonary veins are the only veins that carry oxygenated blood, and they open into the left atrium. Pulmonary arteries take deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.

stem: Antibodies are produced by
options: plasma cells formed from B lymphocytes
explanation: When a B lymphocyte meets its matching antigen it multiplies and forms plasma cells, which secrete large amounts of antibody. Helper T cells regulate the immune response, and neutrophils destroy microbes by phagocytosis.

stem: A person bitten by a snake is injected with antiserum containing ready-made antibodies against the venom. This gives
explanation: The antibodies are made by another animal and given by injection, so the immunity is passive (the body makes none itself) and artificial; it works at once but lasts only a short time. A vaccine would give artificial active immunity, and antibodies crossing the placenta give natural passive immunity.

stem: Lymph collected from the tissues is finally returned to the blood when the thoracic duct empties into the
explanation: Lymph vessels collect excess tissue fluid and drain it through lymph nodes into the thoracic duct, which opens into the left subclavian vein near the heart. This keeps blood volume steady and prevents oedema.

stem: The chamber of the human heart with the thickest muscular wall is the
explanation: The left ventricle pumps blood through the aorta to the whole body, so it must produce the highest pressure. The right ventricle pumps only to the nearby lungs, so its wall is thinner.
